blue: Welcome to Whale Radio. I'm Auntie CeCe. We are nine hundred meters down in Monterey Bay, listening to the largest animal that has ever lived. A blue whale's song is so deep that most of it sits below human hearing, so we have sped it up ten times. Listen for the pulsing call, then the long moan. Each note can travel hundreds of kilometers through the dark.
fin: This is the heartbeat of the ocean. A fin whale, the second largest animal on Earth, sends one deep pulse after another, about every twenty seconds, like a drum keeping time. We sped it up ten times so you can hear it. Scientists count these pulses to learn when fin whales arrive. Patterns like this are exactly what AI learns to recognize, and the whale wrote them first.
humpback: Now, a humpback whale is singing. This is real speed, nothing changed. Only the males sing, and their songs have themes and phrases, repeated for hours. Here is the wonder. Every whale in a population sings nearly the same song, and the song slowly changes each year, passed from whale to whale like a hit tune. That is culture, under the sea.
orca: Hear those bright calls and whistles? Those are killer whales, orcas, talking to each other in the deep off California. Each orca family has its own dialect of calls, learned from mothers and grandmothers. Researchers use AI to sort thousands of these calls, but it was the orcas who invented the language. Listen closely. Someone is answering someone.
dolphin: Clicks, buzzes and whistles. These are dolphins, and they see with sound. Each click bounces off fish and rocks, and the echo paints a picture in the dolphin's mind. Some dolphins even have signature whistles that work like names. The sea is not silent. It is full of conversations we are only now learning to hear.
palaoa: Now we travel to the bottom of the world, under the Ekstrom Ice Shelf in Antarctica, in the dark of winter. Those long falling whistles, like a spaceship coming down, are most likely Weddell seals, singing under the ice. The scientists named this station PALAOA, a Hawaiian word for whale. In the deep polar night, sound is how life finds life.
spac_blue: Out in the open Pacific, eight degrees south of the equator, a hydrophone caught this in 1996. It is a southern blue whale, and its song is different from the Monterey blue whales. Blue whales in different oceans sing different songs, so scientists can tell populations apart just by listening. It is sped up ten times and played twice, so you can hear its shape.
atl_blue: This one comes from the middle of the Atlantic, from a hydrophone moored along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. An Atlantic blue whale moans, low and steady, for about sixteen seconds. We sped it up ten times and played it three times. Imagine that voice crossing an ocean. Every one of these songs reminds us that the universe is full of intelligence, if we take the time to listen.
